abstract: Does breastfeeding transfer living maternal immune cells that persist and function in offspring, beyond providing soluble immune factors? Using a foster-nursing mouse model that eliminates prenatal exposure, this study directly tests whether maternal cells can be transferred postnatally through breastmilk. We found that intact maternal immune cells survive neonatal gastrointestinal transit, enter the circulation, and disseminate to peripheral organs. Single-cell RNA sequencing shows that transferred cells span multiple hematopoietic lineages, dominated by monocyte-derived macrophages with a distinct stress-adapted, inflammatory transcriptional state compatible with persistence in the neonatal environment. Interestingly, these maternal cells are detected at sites of neonatal tissue injury, consistent with chemotactic responsiveness. Our findings suggest that breastfeeding may serve as a postnatal route for maternal cellular transfer, potentially extending maternal immune influence beyond gestation.
